paper.title_en: Transition in Splitting Probabilities of Quantum Walks
paper.abstract_en: We investigate the splitting probability of a monitored continuous-time quantum walk with two targets and show that, in stark contrast to a classical random walk, it exhibits a nonanalytic, phase-transition-like behavior controlled by the sampling time at the targets. For large systems and sampling times smaller than a critical value <math display="inline"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi>τ</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi><mo>/</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>E</mi></mrow></math>, where <math display="inline"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>E</mi></mrow></math> is the energy bandwidth, the splitting probability is universal and equal to <math display="inline"><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></math>, independent of the initial condition and the sampling time. Above the critical sampling time, a nonuniversal regime emerges in which the splitting probability deviates from <math display="inline"><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></math> and develops a fluctuating pattern of pronounced peaks and dips dependent on both the sampling time and the initial condition. These results follow from a nontrivial mapping of the splitting problem onto a pair of single-target detection problems enabled by the superposition principle.
